section.heading: 4.4. Indeterminate Forms and l’Hospital’s Rule
section.paragraph: Suppose we are trying to analyze the behavior of the function
$$F(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x - 1}$$
Although $$F$$ is not defined when $$x = 1$$ , we need to know how $$F$$ behaves near $$1$$ . In particular, we would like to know the value of the limit
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{\ln x}{x - 1}$$

In computing this limit we can’t apply Law 5 of limits (the limit of a quotient is the quotient of the limits, see Section 2.3) because the limit of the denominator is $$0$$ . In fact, although the limit in (1) exists, its value is not obvious because both numerator and denominator approach $$0$$ and $$\frac{0}{0}$$ is not defined.
section.heading: Indeterminate Forms (Types 0 0 , ∞ ∞ )
section.paragraph: In general, if we have a limit of the form
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$

where both $$\left. f(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and $$\left. g(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$ , then this limit may or may not exist and is called an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ . We met some limits of this type in Chapter 2. For rational functions, we can cancel common factors:
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{2} - x}{x^{2} - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x(x - 1)}{(x + 1)(x - 1)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x}{x + 1} = \frac{1}{2}$$
In Section 3.3 we used a geometric argument to show that
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$$
But these methods do not work for limits such as (1).
Another situation in which a limit is not obvious occurs when we look for a horizontal asymptote of $$F$$ and need to evaluate the limit
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x - 1}$$

It isn’t obvious how to evaluate this limit because both numerator and denominator become large as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . There is a struggle between numerator and denominator. If the numerator wins, the limit will be $$\infty$$ (the numerator was increasing significantly faster than the denominator); if the denominator wins, the answer will be $$0$$ . Or there may be some compromise, in which case the answer will be some finite positive number.
In general, if we have a limit of the form
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$$

where both $$\left. f{(x)}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ (or $$- \infty$$ ) and $$\left. g{(x)}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ (or $$- \infty$$ ), then the limit may or may not exist and is called an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ . We saw in Section 2.6 that this type of limit can be evaluated for certain functions, including rational functions, by dividing numerator and denominator by the highest power of $$x$$ that occurs in the denominator. For instance,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - 1}{2x^{2} + 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{2 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}} = \frac{1 - 0}{2 + 0} = \frac{1}{2}$$
But this method does not work for limits such as (2).
section.heading: L’Hospital’s Rule
section.paragraph: We now introduce a systematic method, known as l’Hospital’s Rule, for the evaluation of indeterminate forms of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or type $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ .

section.paragraph: Note 1 L’Hospital’s Rule says that the limit of a quotient of functions is equal to the limit of the quotient of their derivatives, provided that the given conditions are satisfied. It is especially important to verify the conditions regarding the limits of $$f$$ and $$g$$ before using l’Hospital’s Rule.

Note 2 L’Hospital’s Rule is also valid for one-sided limits and for limits at infinity or negative infinity; that is, “ $$\left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$ ” can be replaced by any of the symbols $$\left. x\rightarrow a^{+} \right.$$ , $$\left. x\rightarrow a^{-} \right.$$ , $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , or $$\left. x\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ .

Note 3 For the special case in which $$f(a) = g(a) = 0$$ , $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, and $$g^{\prime}(a) \neq 0$$ , it is easy to see why l’Hospital’s Rule is true. In fact, using the alternative form of the definition of a derivative (2.7.5), we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}} = {\frac{f^{\prime}(a)}{g^{\prime}(a)} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f{(x)} - f{(a)}}{x - a}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{g{(x)} - g{(a)}}{x - a}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{\frac{f{(x)} - f{(a)}}{x - a}}{\frac{g{(x)} - g{(a)}}{x - a}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{g^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{g(x) - g(a)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \left\lbrack {{because}f(a) = g(a) = 0} \right\rbrack}} \end{array}$$
It is more difficult to prove the general version of l’Hospital’s Rule. See Appendix F.

section.heading: Indeterminate Products (Type 0 · ∞ )
section.paragraph: If $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = 0$$ and $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = \infty$$ (or $$- \infty$$ ), then it isn’t clear what the value of $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack$$ , if any, will be. There is a struggle between $$f$$ and $$g$$ . If $$f$$ wins, the answer will be $$0$$ ; if $$g$$ wins, the answer will be $$\infty$$ (or $$- \infty$$ ). Or there may be a compromise where the answer is a finite nonzero number. For instance,
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x^{2} = 0, \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1}{x} = \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x = 0$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x^{2} = 0, \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1}{x^{2}} = \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x \cdot \frac{1}{x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1}{x} = \infty$$
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x = 0, \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1}{x} = \infty$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x \cdot \frac{1}{x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}1 = 1$$
This kind of limit is called an indeterminate form of type $$0 \cdot \mathbf{\infty}$$ . We can deal with it by writing the product $$fg$$ as a quotient:
$$fg = \frac{f}{1 \slash g}$$
or
$$fg = \frac{g}{1 \slash f}$$
This converts the given limit into an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ so that we can use l’Hospital’s Rule.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Solution The given limit is indeterminate because, as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , the first factor $$(x)$$ approaches $$0$$ while the second factor $$\left( {\ln x} \right)$$ approaches $$- \infty$$ . Writing $$x = 1 \slash \left( {1 \slash x} \right)$$ , we have $$\left. 1 \slash x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ , so l’Hospital’s Rule gives

$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x\ln x = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{\ln x}{1 \slash x} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1 \slash x}{- 1 \slash x^{2}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {- x} \right) = 0$$
Figure 5 shows the graph of the function in Example 6. Notice that the function is undefined at $$x = 0$$ ; the graph approaches the origin but never quite reaches it.

section.paragraph: Note In solving Example 6 another possible option would have been to write
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}x\ln x = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{x}{1 \slash \ln x}$$

This gives an indeterminate form of the type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ , but if we apply l’Hospital’s Rule we get a more complicated expression than the one we started with. In general, when we rewrite an indeterminate product, we try to choose the option that leads to the simpler limit.
section.heading: Indeterminate Differences (Type ∞ - ∞ )
section.paragraph: If $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = \infty$$ and $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = \infty$$ , then the limit
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) - g(x)} \right\rbrack$$

is called an indeterminate form of type $$\infty - \infty$$ . Again there is a contest between $$f$$ and $$g$$ . Will the answer be $$\infty$$ ( $$f$$ wins) or will it be $$- \infty$$ ( $$g$$ wins) or will they compromise on a finite number? To find out, we try to convert the difference into a quotient (for instance, by using a common denominator, or rationalization, or factoring out a common factor) so that we have an indeterminate form of type $$\frac{0}{0}$$ or $$\frac{\infty}{\infty}$$ .

section.heading: Indeterminate Powers (Types 0 0 , ∞ 0 , 1 ∞ )
section.paragraph: Several indeterminate forms arise from the limit
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a} = \left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{g{(x)}}$$
Each of these three cases can be treated either by taking the natural logarithm:
$${let}y = \left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{g{(x)}}, {then} \ln y = g(x)\ln f(x)$$
or by using Formula 1.5.10 to write the function as an exponential:
$$\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{g{(x)}} = e^{ g{(x)}\ln f{(x)}}$$
(Recall that both of these methods were used in differentiating such functions.) In either method we are led to the indeterminate product $$g(x)\ln f(x)$$ , which is of type $$0 \cdot \infty$$ .
Although forms of the type $$0^{0}$$ , $$\infty^{0}$$ , and $$1^{\infty}$$ are indeterminate, the form $$0^{\infty}$$ is not indeterminate. (See Exercise 88.)

section.heading: Writing Project The Origins of L’Hospital’s Rule
section.paragraph: L’Hospital’s Rule was first published in 1696 in the Marquis de l’Hospital’s calculus textbook Analyse des infiniment petits, but the rule was discovered in 1694 by the Swiss mathematician John (Johann) Bernoulli. The explanation is that these two mathematicians had entered into a curious business arrangement whereby the Marquis de l’Hospital bought the rights to Bernoulli’s mathematical discoveries. The details, including a translation of l’Hospital’s letter to Bernoulli proposing the arrangement, can be found in the book by Eves [1].

section.paragraph: Write an essay on the historical and mathematical origins of l’Hospital’s Rule. Start by providing brief biographical details of both men (the dictionary edited by Gillispie [2] is a good source) and outline the business deal between them. Then give l’Hospital’s statement of his rule, which is found in Struik’s source book [4] and more briefly in the book of Katz [3]. Notice that l’Hospital and Bernoulli formulated the rule geometrically and gave the answer in terms of differentials. Compare their statement with the version of l’Hospital’s Rule given in Section 4.4 and show that the two statements are essentially the same.

note.title: L’Hospital
note.heading: L’Hospital
note.paragraph: L’Hospital’s Rule is named after a French nobleman, the Marquis de l’Hospital (1661–1704), but was discovered by a Swiss mathematician, John Bernoulli (1667–1748). You might sometimes see l’Hospital spelled as l’Hôpital, but he spelled his own name l’Hospital, as was common in the 17th century. See Exercise 85 for the example that the Marquis used to illustrate his rule. See the project for further historical details.
